Cook and mash the potato, mix while still hot with grated cheddar until melted.
Roll the dough thin, cut circles, fill and close into a half-moon, pinching the edges well.
Poach the perogies in salted boiling water 5 minutes until they float.
Brown the poached perogies in butter with the caramelised onion, serve with the remaining sour cream.

alberta-beef-steak.d: A thick steak from grass-fed cattle raised on Alberta's vast prairies, simply grilled with salt and pepper to let the meat's quality speak for itself, a regional pride celebrated every year at the Calgary Stampede.
s: Take the steak out of the fridge 45 minutes before cooking so it reaches room temperature.
Season generously with coarse salt and cracked pepper on both sides.
Heat a cast-iron pan over very high heat until smoking.
Sear the steak 3 to 4 minutes per side depending on thickness, basting with garlic and thyme butter at the end of cooking.
Let rest 5 minutes under foil before slicing and serving.

nanaimo-bars.d: A cold, no-bake three-layer square, with a crumbled coconut biscuit base, pale yellow buttercream custard, and a crackling dark chocolate topping, a mining town's dessert that became a national emblem.
s: Blitz the biscuits into crumbs, mix with coconut, cocoa and melted butter, add the beaten egg and cook 3 minutes in a bain-marie, stirring.
Press this mixture into a paper-lined square pan, chill 20 minutes.
Beat butter, icing sugar and custard powder until light, spread over the cooled base.
Chill another 20 minutes until firm.
Melt the dark chocolate, pour over the custard layer, chill until hardened before cutting into small squares.

bc-spot-prawns.d: Large spot prawns caught in the cold Pacific waters, available for only a few weeks each spring, simply grilled whole in their shells to preserve their sweet, delicate flesh.
s: Leave the prawns whole with their shells on, do not peel.
Mix olive oil, crushed garlic and sliced chilli, brush generously over the prawns.
Heat a grill or griddle over high heat.
Grill the prawns 2 minutes per side until the shell turns pink and the flesh turns opaque.
Drizzle with a squeeze of lemon, scatter with parsley and serve immediately, to be shelled with fingers.

arctic-char-grilled.d: A fish from the icy waters of the Canadian Arctic, a salmon cousin with delicate pink-orange flesh, caught by Inuit communities and simply grilled whole over a wood fire with salt, letting its exceptional freshness speak for itself.
s: Gut and rinse the whole fish, dry thoroughly.
Salt generously inside and out, tuck a few sprigs of dill and lemon rounds into the cavity.
Heat a grill or wood embers until hot but stable.
Grill the whole fish 6 to 7 minutes per side depending on thickness, until the flesh flakes easily.
Drizzle with melted butter and a squeeze of lemon just before serving.

bannock.d: A traditional unleavened flatbread of the Indigenous peoples of northern Canada, cooked in a pan or on a hot stone, sometimes even wrapped around a stick and cooked over a campfire, an essential staple of bush cooking.
s: Mix flour, baking powder and salt in a large bowl.
Gradually add water, mixing until a supple but non-sticky dough forms.
Knead briefly, let rest 10 minutes under a cloth.
Flatten the dough into one or several thick discs about 2 cm.
Cook in an oiled pan over medium heat, 8 minutes per side until golden and cooked through.

montreal-smoked-meat.d: A beef brisket cured in spices then smoked and steamed, less sweet than its New York pastrami cousin, hand-sliced in front of the customer and piled high between two slices of rye bread with mustard.
s: Rub the beef brisket with a mix of coarse salt, crushed garlic and spices, cure chilled 10 days, turning regularly.
Rinse thoroughly, coat with a generous crust of cracked pepper and coriander.
Cold-smoke then hot-smoke for several hours until a black crust forms.
Steam 4 hours until extremely tender.
Hand-slice in front of guests, pile generously between two slices of rye bread spread with mustard.

beavertails.d: A yeasted dough hand-stretched into a flat oval shape resembling a beaver's tail, fried until golden and crackling, covered in cinnamon sugar, sold hot to skaters on the frozen Rideau Canal every winter.
s: Knead flour, yeast, warm milk, egg, sugar and a pinch of salt into a supple dough, let rise 1 hour.
Divide the dough into balls, hand-stretch each into a flat, elongated oval shape.
Fry in hot oil at 180°C 1 minute per side until golden and crackling.
Drain quickly on paper towel.
Brush with melted butter and dust generously with cinnamon sugar, serve immediately, piping hot.

tire-erable.d: Pure maple syrup heated until it thickens into a concentrated syrup, poured in long streams directly onto fresh snow where it sets instantly, rolled around a wooden stick and eaten still warm-cold right at the sugar shack.
s: Pour the pure maple syrup into a large heavy-bottomed pan.
Heat over medium heat until reaching 112°C on a candy thermometer, never stirring.
Prepare a large tray of clean, freshly fallen snow, or crushed ice as a substitute.
Immediately pour long streams of hot syrup onto the packed snow.
Quickly roll each set stream around a wooden stick before it hardens too much, eat right away.
